title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) that compared two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run used gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for deterministic end‑to‑end correctness checks; preregistration adopted shared_initial_candidate semantics so each task pair received a single LLM candidate shared between arms. Execution completed 240 episodes (120 paired tasks) with model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because generation was intentionally shared, these outcomes measure validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than independent generator or repair robustness. We provide artifact‑grounded evidence, an explicit evidence‑to‑claim mapping, a compact nearest‑work comparison, and prescriptive protocol changes required for a discriminating independent‑generation head‑to‑head follow‑up.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes is operationally critical. Production networks require correctness guarantees (reachability, policy isolation, absence of transient safety violations) together with expressiveness across diverse vendor CLIs. Two broad architectures have emerged: (A) translation‑first pipelines that constrain generation into a vendor DSL and use formal verification/solvers to ensure device guarantees, and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines that centralize generation in an LLM and rely on deterministic validators plus bounded repair loops to bound hallucination and unsafe proposals. This study asked a preregistered, narrowly specified head‑to‑head question: for intent‑driven network changes across heterogeneous CLIs and realistic emulator topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness (measured by deterministic validation: reachability and isolation) — (A) translation‑first or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair? The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed a paired design (N = 120 paired tasks), the primary estimand (paired difference in binary end‑to‑end correctness A − B), and the analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1. Critically, the preregistration adopted shared_initial_candidate semantics: each paired task used a single LLM candidate generated once and presented identically to both downstream orchestration arms. That design deliberately isolates downstream validator acceptance parity and excludes generator variance from the confirmatory estimand. We report the preregistered design, exact execution accounting, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts that support an unambiguous interpretation of observed outcomes and of what the run does and does not test.
sections.related_work:
Two research traditions are relevant. Formal translation→verification work emphasizes constrained synthesis with deterministic guarantees and solver‑based repair; core examples include foundational verification and synthesis systems that focus on soundness and tractability [10,11,12]. LLM‑driven NetOps and agentic AIOps work explore flexible generation, tool orchestration, and iterative repair while stressing deterministic validators to bound hallucination [3,4,5]. Nearest‑work comparison (compact):
• INTA (ICNP 2025) [3]: examined intent translation pipelines and LLM agents with independent generation sampling (independent generation: yes; repair loops: limited; validator acceptance: partial; emulator: yes).
• Mahmood & Song (IFIP Networking 2026) [4]: evaluated self‑correcting multi‑agent verifier pipelines with active repair loops (independent generation: yes; repair loops: yes; validator acceptance: emphasized; domain: Kubernetes policy verification).
• Weighted NetKAT and formal verification literature [5,10–12]: provide solver‑based synthesis and formal guarantees (independent generation: not applicable; repair loops: solver‑based; validator acceptance: core).
The present run differs: preregistration, an archived paired design, deterministic per‑task validator traces, and shared_initial_candidate semantics convert the experiment into a validator‑acceptance parity test for identical candidates. The compact matrix above highlights which experimental dimensions each prior work and this run cover (independent generation, repair loops, validator acceptance, emulator/hardware realism).
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen estimands. The study preregistered: primary estimand = paired difference in binary end‑to‑end correctness (A − B), N_confirmatory = 120 paired tasks, generator = gpt‑5‑mini, validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0), adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1, maximum repair_iterations = 1, and analysis = paired_binary_analysis_v1 (bootstrap percentile CIs + exact McNemar). Preregistration and execution contracts are archived with the run and cited in the execution manifest. Shared_initial_candidate semantics. The adapter implemented shared_initial_candidate: orchestration made a single LLM generation per task pair and supplied the identical textual candidate to both architecture arms. Practical consequences appear in the execution manifest: planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, and model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Provider audit in deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms hosted_model_call_event_count = 120 and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false, supporting execution isolation and adherence to contamination controls. Task generation, validator rules, and scoring. Tasks were produced deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each task manifest entry contains intent, initial and required final states, required safe sequences, difficulty metadata, and a canonical reference answer (see execution/task_manifest.jsonl and representative entries such as task‑000001). The validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applies full_intent_constraint_validation: syntactic normalization, required command inclusion, ordering/dependency checks (e.g., make‑before‑break, shutdown→modify→restore), and final state consistency. A configuration passes end‑to‑end correctness only if validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true. Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task‑000XXX‑*.json) record normalized_response, parsed_command_count, validation_before/after snapshots, and repair_applied flags; these are canonical evidence of each scored decision. Analysis executor and statistical specifics. The preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor computed paired contingency counts (n11,n10,n01,n00), paired difference (A − B), a bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729), and an exact McNemar two‑sided test. Analysis artifacts include analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (bootstrap parameters recorded). Hypothesis mapping and preregistered outcomes. The preregistered H1 and H2 were: H1 — translation‑first produces higher end‑to‑end correctness than agentic; H2 — agentic yields higher repair coverage. Because the run used shared_initial_candidate, the experiment measures validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates (the estimand differs from the original broader architecture‑comparison interpretation). We therefore map each preregistered hypothesis to the executed measurand and report test status explicitly (see the Evidence→Claim subsection and Table 3).
sections.results: Execution accounting. The execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) records planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 120 (single shared generation per pair). Deterministic reconciliation confirms complete_pair_count = 120 and provider audit counts consistent with the single shared generation stage. Primary numeric outcomes. Deterministic scoring produced paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Marginal success rates are baseline = 120/120 = 1.0 and guarded = 120/120 = 1.0; paired difference (A − B) = 0.00. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl lists bootstrap_resamples = 10000 and bootstrap_seed = 1729. Exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. All analysis outputs are archived at analysis/results.json and supporting CSVs. Repair and secondary outcomes. Aggregated repair_applied count = 0 for all 240 episodes (execution/scoring/*.json show repair_applied = false). Consequently preregistered secondary estimands concerning repair coverage (H2) are unobserved in this execution. Representative per‑task traces. Representative per‑task JSONs illustrate validator internals and the shared candidate effect: for pair‑000001 the shared candidate matches the canonical reference modulo ordering normalization; execution/scoring/task‑000001‑baseline.json documents normalized_response, parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, validation_after.valid = true, and repair_applied = false. Similar artifacts for additional pairs (task‑000002, task‑000003, …) are archived; excerpts support reproducible verification of the reported counts. Contamination and missingness checks. Preregistered contamination checks produced no flags: analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty and analysis/missingness_summary.csv records complete_pairs = 120 with no observed failures. Provider audit metadata indicates cache_miss_count = 120 and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false, supporting execution isolation per the contamination_plan.
sections.discussion: What the run measured and its scope. By design (preregistered shared_initial_candidate), this experiment isolates downstream validator acceptance parity: given identical LLM candidates, do translation‑first and agentic orchestration pipelines differ in deterministic validator acceptance? The observed degenerate concordance (n11 = 120) answers that restricted question: both validators accepted the identical candidates for every paired task. The run does not exercise independent generator variance, sampling effects, or repair efficacy; claims about which architecture would produce more correct initial candidates when operating independently are therefore untested. Evidence→claim mapping (compact). We provide an explicit mapping from preregistered hypotheses/estimands to executed measurements and archived artifacts: 1) H1 (Paired difference A − B): Measured estimand in this execution = validator‑acceptance parity under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Supporting artifacts: preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1 recorded in execution manifest), execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (n11=120,n10=0,n01=0,n00=0). Verdict: Tested only for validator‑acceptance parity; independent generator comparison remains untested. 2) H2 (Agentic pipeline repair coverage): Measured? No — repair_applied = false for all episodes. Supporting artifacts: execution/scoring/*.json (repair_applied=false per episode), analysis/missingness_summary.csv. Verdict: Unobserved. Operational implications and recommended follow‑ups. This experiment demonstrates a reproducible protocol for validator regression testing and orchestrator equivalence checks when generation is held constant. To discriminate architectures on independent generator and repair performance, the preregistered protocol should be modified (and immediately re‑preregistered): (i) remove shared_initial_candidate so each arm obtains an independent LLM generation per pair — model_calls_used would increase to 240 for initial candidates alone; (ii) allow multiple sampled generations per arm to estimate generator variance (further increasing model_calls); (iii) enable repair iterations and instrument repair_applied counters so repair coverage > 0 can be observed; (iv) increase device fidelity (hardware or higher‑fidelity emulation) to reduce simulator‑to‑hardware contamination risk. Each modification produces verifiable changes in the execution manifest (model_calls_used, hosted_model_call_event_count, nonzero repair_applied flags) and therefore supports clear replication and auditability. Threats to validity (focused). Internal validity: shared_candidate removes generator variance intentionally; this was preregistered and narrows the estimand. Construct validity: deterministic acceptance operationalizes correctness per validator rules but omits human‑facing properties (explainability, maintainability). External validity: synthetic task corpus and Mininet‑derived emulation reduce production generality; single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) restrict model/validator generality. Conclusion validity: degenerate concordance (all pairs concordant) yields a point mass bootstrap CI and p = 1.0; these are correct descriptors but do not imply practical architectural equivalence under independent operation. Reproducibility and artifact access. All artifacts supporting execution, analysis, and claims are archived in the run bundle and referenced by the execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json). Key artifacts cited in this paper include the preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1), execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini), execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/responses/*, execution/scoring/*.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, and analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json. Per‑task validator traces (execution/scoring/task‑000XXX‑*.json) are the canonical evidence for each scored decision and permit automated recomputation of the paired_binary_analysis_v1 outputs using preserved seeds and executor parameters.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, fully archived paired experiment comparing translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair NetOps pipelines under shared_initial_candidate semantics. For 120 paired tasks the deterministic validator accepted the identical LLM candidates in both arms for all pairs (n11 = 120, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0), yielding paired difference 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs were applied (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered hypotheses about repair coverage are therefore unobserved. The run demonstrates how preregistered shared‑candidate experiments precisely measure validator‑acceptance parity but, by design, do not adjudicate independent generator or repair robustness. We supply artifact‑grounded evidence, an explicit evidence→claim mapping in the text and Table 3, a compact nearest‑work comparison, and concrete preregistered protocol modifications that would enable a discriminating independent‑generation head‑to‑head comparison in follow‑ups.

limitations: Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were used; this intentionally removes generator variance and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.

The task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
A single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust, which matter in production but were outside the metric used here.
